planting.note: Traditionally grown as transplanted paddy seedlings once soil and water temperatures are reliably warm after the last frost.

directions: IR8 was bred at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines, released in 1966 as a cross between the Indonesian tall variety Peta and the Chinese semi-dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen. Its short, sturdy stalks resist lodging under heavy fertilization, unlike traditional tall varieties, allowing it to convert nitrogen into grain rather than excess leaf and stem growth. It is photoperiod-insensitive, meaning it can be grown and harvested on a fixed schedule regardless of day length, enabling multiple crops per year. IR8's dramatic yield increase over traditional varieties made it the symbolic starting point of the Green Revolution in Asian rice agriculture.

planting.note: Grown as transplanted paddy seedlings in warm, flooded conditions well after the last frost.

directions: IR36 was released by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the 1970s as a successor to IR8, bred to combine high yield with a broad package of resistances to pests and diseases such as brown planthopper, grassy stunt virus, and bacterial blight. Its shorter growth duration compared to earlier varieties allowed farmers to fit in additional cropping cycles per year in favorable climates. For a period it was reported to be the most widely planted rice variety on Earth, grown across millions of hectares in Asia. Like other IRRI semi-dwarf rices, it is short-statured, lodging-resistant, and responds strongly to fertilizer inputs.

common_name: IR64 Rice (Widely Grown Modern Indica Variety)

planting.note: Transplanted as paddy seedlings into flooded fields once temperatures are consistently warm after the last frost.

directions: IR64 was released by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in 1985, combining good grain quality with high yield, broad disease and pest resistance, and wide adaptability across irrigated lowland environments. It became one of the most extensively grown rice varieties in the history of agriculture, planted across large areas of South and Southeast Asia for decades. Its semi-dwarf stature resists lodging under heavy fertilization, and its photoperiod insensitivity allows flexible planting schedules. IR64 is often used as a benchmark variety in rice breeding research due to its long track record of farmer adoption.

common_name: Norin 10 Wheat (Dwarfing Gene Source for the Green Revolution)

planting.note: Sown as a cool-season cereal, typically in early spring or the prior autumn depending on climate, well before the heat of summer.

directions: Norin 10 is a Japanese semi-dwarf wheat variety developed in Japan and brought to the United States after World War II, where it carried dwarfing genes that produced a much shorter, sturdier stalk than conventional tall wheats. Agronomist Norman Borlaug used Norin 10 derivatives in his breeding program in Mexico to create short-strawed wheats that resisted lodging under heavy fertilization, directly enabling the dramatic yield gains of the wheat Green Revolution. Its short stature allows more of the plant's energy to go into grain rather than straw. Norin 10's dwarfing genes remain present in the pedigree of many modern high-yield wheat varieties worldwide.
sources: CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)

planting.note: Sown as a cool-season irrigated cereal in a window that avoids hard frost on young seedlings but keeps growth ahead of summer heat.

directions: Sonora 64 was bred by Norman Borlaug's program at what became CIMMYT in Mexico and released in 1964 as one of the first widely adopted semi-dwarf, high-yield wheat varieties. It carried dwarfing genes derived from the Japanese variety Norin 10, giving it a short, sturdy straw that resisted lodging even under heavy fertilizer and irrigation inputs that would topple traditional tall wheats. Sonora 64 was photoperiod-insensitive and could be grown successfully across a range of latitudes, which helped it spread rapidly to wheat-growing regions such as India and Pakistan in the mid-1960s. Its substantially higher yields compared to traditional varieties made it a cornerstone of the wheat Green Revolution.
sources: CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)
Norman Borlaug Institute for International Agriculture
